Kristi: Hi, Denise. You wanted to see me?
Denise: Yeah. I came to your desk, but you were out.
Kristi: I'm sorry, I went out for coffee.
Denise: No problem. Anyway, we have received the new children's book from Marisa Mitchell.
Kristi: Winnie's World?
Denise: Yes, you know it?
Kristi: I think it came up once in a meeting.
Denise: Right. I've wondered why she chose that name. Ever since I first heard it, I've been trying to think of another name. It's not my favorite. Anyway, I read it earlier and as you are a junior copy editor and have an interest in children's books, I'm going to get you to review it for me.
Kristi: What did you think of it?
Denise: I'm going to abstain from commenting until after you perused it.

Kristi: You're withholding your opinion because you are afraid it may cloud my judgment?
Denise: Ever since my last assistant, I've been reluctant to reveal my opinions on new manuscripts.
Kristi: In case I just parrot your opinion back to you?
Denise: Exactly! Since I need other opinions that is not an effective strategy. I've been a bit more careful since then.
Kristi: Fair enough. Can you tell me what it's about?
Denise: As I said, I don't want to give too much away but the general gist is it's about a hedgehog who teaches children how to use social media safely. I'm curious to see if we have congruent opinions on it.

Kristi: Ok. Could you tell me a little about the author?
Denise: Marisa Mitchell? She has handed in several manuscripts for us in the past, but this one is the first with any real potential. I've often wondered why she decided to become an author, but I think she might be coming into her own. But let's leave it at that. I've always felt that a good review focuses on the writing not the author.
Kristi: Ok. When would you like it done by?
Denise: Tomorrow if you could.
Kristi: Talk to you tomorrow.

Reason Clauses Using Because, Since, As, For, (Just) In Case

You use a reason clause to refer to what someone intends to do. Although the most common way to talk about purpose is with an infinitive of purpose (to + verb), there are other ways to talk about the reasons people do things.

For example:
I told her to hold off writing the report because the details hadn't been decided on yet.
Here, because answers the question Why?

Since the meeting is going over time, we should order dinner for everyone.
As you may have heard, there is a Christmas party next week.
Here, you use since or as to introduce reasons that the listener already knows.

You should e-mail her the information just in case she forgets it next week.
Here, (just) in case is used to talk about things that may possibly happen.
You're withholding your opinion because you are afraid your opinion may cloud my judgment?
In case I just parrot your opinion back to you?
The Present Perfect: Commenting on the Present Results of Something in the Past
You use the Present Perfect to talk about past actions that have a connection to the present.
When you want to comment on the present results of a past action, you can use the Present Perfect with verbs like appear, seem and sound.

For example:
It sounds as if you've already decided on the next course of action.
It seems they have completed the report ahead of schedule.

The form of the Present Perfect is:
subject + has/have + past participle
You can use some typical expressions with the Present Perfect like just, recently, already, lately, before, so far, etc.
I've wondered why she chose that name.
I've been a bit more careful since then.
Ever since my last assistant, I've been reluctant to reveal my opinions on new manuscripts.
